title: I Built AI Test Automation. Today, I Went Back to Manual Testing.

content_html:
Today, I manually tested a project.

It doesn't sound like anything special.

After all, I've been working in software testing for 16 years. Manual testing used to be a big part of my everyday work. But recently, the way I work has changed quite a bit.

I've built an AI-powered test automation framework at my company, and quite a few projects are now being tested by AI.

From understanding requirements and designing test scenarios to interacting with applications, exploring edge cases, organizing test results, and reporting bugs, AI can now handle many tasks that used to take QA engineers a lot of time.

I know what this framework can do. I've watched it gradually change the way our team works.

So today, when I opened a project and started clicking through the screens, checking things one by one, and looking for problems myself, I found myself thinking about something I hadn't expected.

A Very Simple Bug Report

I found a few issues today and submitted them to our bug tracking system as usual.

But compared with the reports generated by AI, mine were pretty basic.

AI usually produces much more detailed reports. It can organize the testing context, list reproduction steps, describe expected and actual results, attach relevant screenshots and page information, and sometimes even provide an initial analysis of what might have gone wrong.

My reports today were much simpler.

A straightforward title, a few reproduction steps, and a description of what actually happened. A screenshot when necessary.

No lengthy analysis. No particularly elaborate structure.

Just ordinary bug reports.

But the problems were real, and someone still needed to find them and report them.

It suddenly occurred to me that I'd become so used to AI making test results more complete and detailed that seeing my own simple reports today made me think of all the QA engineers who still spend their days finding problems one by one.

Please Appreciate the QA Engineers Who Still Test by Hand

I'm not trying to bring back manual testing.

Quite the opposite. I've been pushing for AI test automation, and I hope more repetitive and time-consuming testing tasks can be handed over to AI.

I know how much efficiency automation can bring.

But today, I suddenly wanted to say something to developers:

Please appreciate the QA engineers who are still testing by hand.

When they submit a bug report, it may not be as detailed as one written by AI. The reproduction steps may not look as polished, and the analysis may not be as complete.

But don't underestimate the time and effort behind finding that issue just because the report looks simple.

What you see might be only a title and a few steps to reproduce the problem.

Before submitting it, the QA engineer may have already tried many things, switched between pages and test data, and explored different paths before confirming that the issue was worth reporting.

Sometimes, finding a seemingly simple bug isn't simple at all.

If the description isn't clear enough, ask the QA engineer for more details. If you can't reproduce it, work together to figure out what's happening.

That's what collaboration between development and QA should look like.

Don't let a simple bug report become a reason to take someone's work less seriously.

AI Will Change Testing, But It Shouldn't Change How We Treat People

I believe more and more projects will adopt AI-powered test automation.

Maybe one day, most routine testing will no longer need to be performed manually by QA engineers.

I hope that day comes, too.

But until then, there are still plenty of QA engineers opening pages by hand, entering data, clicking buttons, and checking results. They may not have sophisticated automation tools or beautiful reports generated by AI. They simply rely on their experience and patience to check, again and again, whether the product works as expected.

Their work may not look exciting, and it may never make it into a company's AI transformation presentation.

But they're still taking responsibility for product quality.

Technological progress should never be a reason to overlook the people who are doing their jobs with care.

Today, while submitting those simple bug reports, I found myself thinking about all the QA engineers who are still doing manual testing.

I'll keep pushing AI test automation and finding more ways to let AI handle testing work.

I just hope that the next time a developer receives a bug report from someone doing manual testing, they'll show a little more patience and understanding.

After all, until AI takes over all the testing, there's still someone sitting in front of a screen, clicking through the application and checking things again and again.

That person deserves to be seen.

And deserves to be treated with respect.
